1:
Where Sheba was is settled by Ellicott on a point of spelling that the others miss. Sheba must be distinguished from Seba, which begins with a different Hebrew letter and denotes a Cushite race connected in the prophets with Egypt and Cush; and it is probably from confusion between the two, he says, that Josephus makes this a queen of Egypt and Ethiopia. Gill reports that opinion of Josephus and rejects it without diagnosing it, placing Sheba in the southern part of Arabia Felix and collecting the names given her in other traditions, including Maqueda among the Ethiopians and a title that amounts to queen of the south. Clarke reaches the same region by way of our Lord's phrase queen of the south. Henry notes that the Christians in Ethiopia are to this day confident she came from their country, but thinks Arabia the more probable. Ellicott's conclusion goes further than any of them: since the kingdom must be the Joktanite one, the queen was of Semitic race and so not wholly an alien from the stock of Abraham.

What the hard questions were divides them sharply. Clarke renders the word riddles and observes that riddles, problems, fables and apologues formed the principal part of Eastern wisdom, and are delighted in still. Ellicott dismisses the Arabian legends, whose list of puzzles he calls too puerile to be worth mention, and argues that what is meant must be the enigmatic and metaphorical sayings in which Eastern philosophy tersely embodies the results of speculation, moral and religious, of the kind that occupy Job, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. Delitzsch denies exactly that: there is no ground, he says, for thinking of sayings of a religious nature, as the earlier commentators supposed, but simply of sayings whose meaning was concealed. Henry is on Ellicott's side and pushes further, taking it that what she chiefly aimed at was instruction in the things of God, since the fame she had heard concerned the name of the Lord.

The last item in the list of what overwhelmed her is a translation crux, and Clarke is blunt about it. He finds it very strange that steps up to the temple should be a separate matter of astonishment, and points out that the Vulgate, the Greek, the Chaldee, the Syriac and the Arabic all render the phrase as the burnt offerings which Solomon offered in the house of the Lord, as does the German; from which, in this place, he says our version has most pitifully departed. Henry records the same alternative without choosing, though he plainly likes what it yields, an ascent made with as much humility as he showed majesty at other times. Delitzsch leaves the ascent standing but corrects a different word in the same list, taking it not of cupbearers, as the Greek and Latin have it, but of the drink, and so of the whole drinking arrangements.

That there was no more spirit in her Clarke treats as a physical fact rather than a figure. She was overpowered and fainted, he says, and this is a natural and not an uncommon effect; he reports having seen it himself, when a lady who was an artist, viewing some exquisitely finished oriental paintings, twice nearly fainted and had to leave the room. Delitzsch turns instead to what her blessing of God implies, noting that the earlier theologians inferred from it, taken with our Lord's words about her, that the queen had been converted to the true God. Henry does not press the question but reads her speech as a lesson to the king she was praising, since she attributed his prosperity not to his wisdom but to his doing judgment and justice, and both magistrates and ministers must be more solicitous to do the duty of their places than to secure the honours and profits of them.
11:
Gill and Delitzsch agree that the navy is mentioned here by association rather than sequence, the costly presents just described leading the historian to add what else came from Ophir. Gill supplies a motive for the insertion that Delitzsch does not: it shows that Solomon had not his gold, or at least not all of it, from the queen of Sheba, but much from Hiram. He adds that Ophir lay in India, and lists the classical authors who report gold in that part of the world.

What the almug trees were nobody can say, and Clarke works through the versions rather than deciding. He notes first that the Chronicles parallel spells the word algum, the two middle letters transposed, and thinks that form probably the more correct. The Vulgate makes it the thya or lignum vitae, and he passes on the derivation that would explain the name from the wood's being so close in texture that it can imbibe no water. The Greek makes it pine timber, the Syriac probably cypress, and the Arabic coloured wood, adding by way of paraphrase that the wood was by nature painted with various colours. That last Clarke thinks comes nearest the truth, taking it for wood shaded in different colours such as the rose woods brought from the East Indies, and he observes that for inlaying and veneering nothing can be finer.

What was made of it is a second crux, and here Delitzsch clears the ground by rejecting three rival readings in turn. The word signifies a support, and the second term may be a later form for a flight of steps, so that what is meant is steps with bannisters. Divans he dismisses as quite out of place in the temple; narrow panelled strips on the floor cannot in the smallest degree be deduced from the word; and moveables such as tables, benches, footstools, boxes and drawers agree neither with the temple, where there was no such furniture, nor with the reading in Chronicles. Gill reaches the same general sense by a different route and ties it back to the queen's visit: the ascent or causeway Solomon made from his own house to the temple, whose pavement on one authority, or whose supports, or rather the rails on either side by which men steadied themselves as they passed, were made of this wood. Since that ascent was what she admired, Gill says, it is particularly observed here what wood it was made of.

The parting gift draws three readings of the same phrase. Ellicott hears in the terms a position of inferiority, well graced and honoured but inferior still, so that what she brought was of the nature of tribute, and he notes the custom behind Solomon giving whatever she asked, since in the East a thing is asked for by being praised. Delitzsch makes it decorous reciprocity instead, the gifts given according to the hand, that is the might, of the king, over and above the return presents that Oriental custom obliged him to make for hers. Clarke reports what neither of them will touch, that some imagine what she desired was progeny, and that the traditions of her own country hold she bore Solomon a son named Menilek, who was brought up at the Israelite court, succeeded her in the kingdom, and introduced the Jewish religion among his subjects.
14:
Four commentators price the 666 talents and produce four different figures. Delitzsch makes it more than seventeen million thalers, which he glosses as two and a half million sterling; Clarke reckons it at over four and a half million sterling; Gill gives two valuations from other authorities, one in pounds and one in ducats. Ellicott alone shows his working, and the working matters. If the talent here is the gold talent of a hundred manehs, each of a hundred shekels, then on the figures preserved in Josephus the whole comes to gold worth nearly eight million; but the silver talent is expressly three thousand sanctuary shekels, and on that standard the same 666 talents give little more than half as much. Since the verse says plainly that this sum is independent of the customs and tributes that follow, Ellicott judges the smaller figure the likelier. He then offers a reason the size need not be incredible: accumulations of gold have at times been great enough to reduce its value in practice and turn it from currency into ornament, as among the Mexicans and Peruvians before the Spanish conquests.

Delitzsch guards the figure from two misreadings. It is evidently a round number resting on an approximate valuation, and it cannot mean strictly every single year, since the Ophir fleet came only once in three; nor can it be confined to direct taxes on Israelites, since it takes in commerce by sea and land, the royal domains, and the presents of foreign princes. Henry is the only one who notices the number itself, calling it an ominous one and pointing the reader to Revelation. Ellicott adds a note about the governors named in the next verse: the word is used constantly of foreign satraps, so it means governors of tributary countries rather than officers within Israel, and may well be a word later than the age of Solomon, introduced by the compiler.

On the shields the technical and the moral readings sit side by side. Delitzsch explains that ancient shields were of wood or basket-work plated with gold instead of leather, and that beaten gold means gold drawn out rather than alloyed; six hundred shekels would weigh about seventeen and a half pounds. Gill observes that the Carthaginians likewise made shields of gold. Henry alone asks what they were for, and answers that they were not for service but for state; and he makes the contrast tell, that magistrates have swords and maces borne before them, in token of power to punish, whereas Solomon had shields carried before him to signify that he took more pleasure in protecting the good, magistrates being shields of the earth.

The throne draws the fullest description. Delitzsch insists it was not made of ivory but ornamented with it, the gold laid upon the wood and the ivory set within the gold plate. Ellicott traces the ivory to the Tyrians, who drew it through Arabia from India, observes that the only other ivory in the history is Ahab's ivory house and that Ahab too was allied with Tyre, and supposes the work itself Tyrian. His reading of the ornament is precise: the lion was the emblem of Judah, the twelve answered to the tribes, and the sheer height of the throne was itself the emblem of majesty in a country where men commonly sat on the ground. He adds that an Assyrian throne from a relief at Nineveh has horses where this has lions. Henry takes the lions as a memorandum to the king of the courage with which he ought to execute judgment, not fearing the face of man. The cargo of the Tharshish fleet troubles him, though: gold and silver and ivory are substantial and serviceable goods, but apes to play with and peacocks to look at suggest to him a people by now overcharged with prosperity and grown childish.
23:
Delitzsch begins with a verb. The text says that Solomon became greater than all the kings of the earth, not that he was greater, and the tense makes these two verses look back to 1 Kings 5:14. He reads the presents plainly: gold and silver vessels, court dresses of a kind still given in the East, armour, spices, horses and mules. Clarke takes the same list as tribute and reads each item for what it tells us about the country, armour being hardly made in Judea and horses rare. Gill does not stop at the sum: in this eminence Solomon was a type of Christ.

On the chariots Ellicott is the only one who asks what they were doing in this chapter at all, and answers that they are noticed here among the commerce and the wealth as one of the powers that held the kingdom together, the chariot cities being fortified posts. Over silver made common as the stones the commentators divide. Gill calls it simply a hyperbole and Delitzsch agrees, adding that the sycomores to which the cedars are compared are rare in Palestine now though anciently they abounded in the lowlands; Clarke reads it as a loss rather than a gain, that Solomon destroyed the value of silver by making it so exceedingly plentiful. Ellicott turns it into politics: the influx enriched Jerusalem and the court, since the tribute and the commerce were in the king's hands alone, and such enrichment can leave the general population impoverished and oppressed, which is why interest and allegiance divided at the accession of Rehoboam.

The horses out of Egypt raise two questions, one moral and one textual. Gill observes only that it seems contrary to the command; Clarke says it outright, that God had absolutely prohibited the importing of horses and that in many things Solomon paid little attention to the divine command. The textual question is the word rendered linen yarn, which Clarke thinks hard to understand if it is not corrupt, and he lays out five attempts on it: the Vulgate and the Septuagint make it a place name, Bochart makes it the tribute farmed out at a price, some make it the cord by which one horse's head is tied to the tail of another, Jarchi makes it a drove or stud, and Houbigant emends it to chariots, which Clarke grants makes the best sense but is supported by no version and no manuscript yet collated. As the text stands he prefers Bochart. Ellicott calls the words an error and prefers the Septuagint reading from Tekoa, a town which would serve well as an emporium for caravans; he adds that Egypt abounded in horses although they appear on no monument before the eighteenth dynasty, so that they may have come in with the Hyksos.

At the prices Gill does the conversion and then corrects himself, six hundred shekels coming to seventy-five pounds at half a crown but a shekel being worth no more than two shillings and fourpence farthing. Delitzsch warns against the obvious inference: a chariot here means the car with its team, and one cannot divide six hundred by a hundred and fifty to get the number of horses, since the car itself would not have been thrown in; so he declines both the four-horse team and the two-and-two reserve reading. Clarke supposes the Hittite kings the remnant of the old inhabitants of Canaan, gone north and formed into a principality, and Ellicott confirms it from Egyptian and Assyrian inscriptions that describe a powerful Hittite confederacy in the valley of the Orontes. Henry refuses to admire it, recalling that the man who exceeded all the kings of the earth had asked at the outset not for wealth or honour but for an understanding heart, and that having tasted all of this he wrote a whole book to show the vanity of it.
